tool.name: Scala
tool.tagline: Expressive JVM language fusing functional and object-oriented programming
tool.description: Scala is a statically typed language for the JVM (and JavaScript and native) that combines object-oriented and functional programming with a powerful type system and concise syntax. It powers data and streaming platforms such as Apache Spark, Kafka tooling and Akka/Pekko systems, as well as backend services at many companies. Learning Scala 3 teaches you immutable data modelling, pattern matching, type classes and safe concurrency that carry over to any language.

concepts.name: Running Scala and @main
concepts.summary: Run Scala 3 programs with the scala command (Scala CLI), write a @main method and use the REPL.
concepts.why: You need a fast edit-run loop before learning anything else.
concepts.body:
Since Scala 3.5 the `scala` command is **Scala CLI**: one tool that compiles, runs, tests and packages code. Install it (with Coursier, Homebrew or SDKMAN), then `scala run hello.scala` compiles and runs a file, `scala repl` (or just `scala`) opens the interactive REPL, and `scala test .` runs tests. Larger projects use **sbt**, Mill or Gradle, covered later.

A program's entry point is any top-level method annotated `@main`. Its parameters are parsed from the command line, so `@main def greet(name: String, times: Int)` can be run with `scala run greet.scala -- Ana 2`; the compiler generates the parsing and an error message for bad input.

Scala 3 code can be written with **significant indentation** (Python-like, the default style) or with braces; both compile. `if`/`then`, `while`/`do` and `for`/`do` read naturally without parentheses. An `end` marker such as `end greet` is optional and helps in long blocks.

Directives at the top of a file configure Scala CLI: `//> using scala 3.7` picks the version and `//> using dep com.lihaoyi::os-lib:0.11.4` adds a library, so a single file can be a complete script.

Top-level definitions (methods, values, types) are allowed in Scala 3; no wrapper object is needed. Files ending in `.sc` are scripts that may also contain top-level statements, run in order; the short examples in these lessons that have no `@main` are written that way (or paste them into the REPL).
takeaways: `scala run file.scala` compiles and runs; `scala` alone opens the REPL
`@main` methods are entry points with parsed arguments
Indentation syntax and braces are both valid Scala 3
`//> using` directives declare the Scala version and dependencies
pitfalls: Forgetting `--` before program arguments, so Scala CLI tries to interpret them as its own options.

quiz.q: What does @main def run(n: Int) do when the program is started with the argument abc?
options: It throws a NumberFormatException with a stack trace
It prints an error about the illegal Int argument
quiz.explain: The compiler-generated wrapper parses arguments and reports invalid ones with an error message.

concepts.name: Values, variables and types
concepts.summary: val versus var, type inference, the basic types and string interpolation.
concepts.why: Immutability by default and inferred static types shape all Scala code.
concepts.body:
`val x = 10` defines an **immutable** value; `var y = 10` a mutable variable you can reassign. Idiomatic Scala uses `val` almost everywhere: values that never change are easier to reason about and safe to share between threads.

Types are **inferred**, so `val x = 10` is an `Int`, but you can annotate: `val ratio: Double = 0.5`. Annotate public method results and anything where the inferred type isn't obvious.

The basic types are `Int`, `Long`, `Double`, `Float`, `Boolean`, `Char`, `String`, `Byte`, `Short`, plus `BigInt` and `BigDecimal` for arbitrary precision. They're all objects with methods (`1.to(5)`, `"abc".reverse`), but compile to JVM primitives where possible. `Unit` (written `()`) is the type of expressions with no useful value, like `println`.

The type hierarchy has `Any` at the top, with `AnyVal` (number-like types) and `AnyRef` (objects, i.e. `java.lang.Object`) below it, and `Nothing` at the bottom: the type of `throw` and of expressions that never return.

**String interpolation**: `s"Hi $name, ${a + b}"` inserts values, `f"$pi%.2f"` formats printf-style with type checking, and `raw"..."` skips escapes. Triple quotes `"""..."""` make multi-line strings; `.stripMargin` removes leading `|` margins.

`==` compares values (it calls `equals`), so string comparison just works; `eq` checks reference identity.
concepts.code:
val name = "Ada"
var visits = 1
visits += 1
// name = "Bob"            // error: Reassignment to val name

val pi: Double = math.Pi
val big = BigInt(2).pow(100)
println(s"$name visited $visits times")   // Ada visited 2 times
println(f"pi is $pi%.3f")                 // pi is 3.142
println(s"2^100 = ${big.toString.length} digits")  // 2^100 = 31 digits

val a = "scala"
val b = "sca" + "la".trim
println(a == b)                           // true (value equality)
println(7 / 2)                            // 3 (Int division)
println(7 / 2.0)                          // 3.5
println("""|multi
           |line""".stripMargin)          // multi / line
takeaways: Prefer `val`; use `var` only for local, contained mutation
Types are inferred; annotate public APIs
`s"..."` interpolates, `f"..."` formats with type checks
`==` is value equality, `eq` is reference identity
pitfalls: Integer division: `7 / 2` is 3; make one operand a Double for 3.5.

quiz.q: What happens when you reassign a val?
quiz.explain: A val can't be reassigned; the compiler rejects it.

quiz.q: In Scala, what does "ab" == "a" + "b" evaluate to?
quiz.explain: == delegates to equals, so strings with the same content are equal.

concepts.name: Expressions and control structures
concepts.summary: if, while, for loops and blocks, where almost everything is an expression that returns a value.
concepts.why: Thinking in expressions instead of statements is what makes Scala code concise.
concepts.body:
In Scala nearly everything is an **expression** with a value. `if` returns a value, so there's no ternary operator: `val sign = if x < 0 then -1 else 1`. A block `{ ... }` (or an indented block) evaluates to its last expression. An `if` without `else` yields `()` when the condition is false, so its value is rarely useful.

Loops:

- `while cond do body` is the imperative loop; it returns `Unit`.
- `for i <- 1 to 5 do println(i)` iterates over a range or collection. `1 to 5` includes 5, `1 until 5` excludes it, and `by` sets a step.
- Several generators and guards can be combined: `for i <- 1 to 3; j <- 1 to 3 if i != j do ...`.
- `for x <- xs yield f(x)` builds a new collection: a **for expression**. Its result type follows the input collection.

`match` is the other key control structure (covered in pattern matching): `x match { case 1 => "one"; case _ => "many" }`.

There is no `break` or `continue` keyword. Usually a collection method (`find`, `takeWhile`, `exists`) expresses the intent better; `scala.util.boundary` with `break` exists for the rare cases you need an early exit.

`try`/`catch`/`finally` is an expression too, and `return` is rarely used: the last expression of a method is its result.
concepts.code:
val x = -7
val sign = if x < 0 then "negative" else "non-negative"
println(sign)                               // negative

val total =
  val a = 10
  val b = 32
  a + b                                     // value of the block
println(total)                              // 42

var n = 1
while n < 100 do n *= 3
println(n)                                  // 243

for i <- 1 to 3; j <- 1 to 3 if i < j do
  print(s"($i,$j) ")                        // (1,2) (1,3) (2,3)
println()

val squares = for k <- 1 until 5 yield k * k
println(squares)                            // Vector(1, 4, 9, 16)
println((10 to 1 by -3).toList)             // List(10, 7, 4, 1)
takeaways: `if`, blocks, `match`, `try` and `for ... yield` all return values
`1 to n` includes n, `1 until n` excludes it
`for ... do` loops for effects, `for ... yield` builds collections
pitfalls: Writing an `if` without `else` and expecting a useful value: the missing branch is `()`.

quiz.q: What is the type of if (cond) 42 with no else branch?
options: Unit or Any depending on cond
quiz.explain: Without else the missing branch is Unit, and the least upper bound of Int and Unit is AnyVal.

concepts.name: Methods and function values
concepts.summary: Define methods with def, use default and named arguments, and pass functions as values.
concepts.why: Functions as values are the basis of the collections API and of functional style.
concepts.body:
A **method** is defined with `def`: `def area(w: Double, h: Double = 1.0): Double = w * h`. Parameter types are required, the result type is usually inferred but should be written on public methods, and the body is a single expression (or an indented block). Callers can use **named arguments** in any order (`area(h = 2, w = 3)`) and skip parameters with defaults.

Methods can have several parameter lists, `def add(a: Int)(b: Int) = a + b`, useful for type inference, `using` clauses and passing blocks: `retry(3) { ... }`. A parameter typed `=> A` is **by-name**: evaluated each time it's used rather than before the call, which lets you write control-structure-like methods.

A **function value** (lambda) is written `(x: Int) => x * 2`. When the expected type is known you can drop the types, `xs.map(x => x * 2)`, or use the placeholder shorthand `xs.map(_ * 2)`. Function types read naturally: `Int => Int`, `(String, Int) => Boolean`.

Methods are converted to functions automatically when a function is expected (**eta-expansion**), so `xs.map(area(_, 2))` or `names.foreach(println)` just work.

Varargs use `*`: `def sum(xs: Int*) = xs.sum`, and a sequence is passed with `sum(list*)`.
concepts.code:
def area(w: Double, h: Double = 1.0): Double = w * h
println(area(3))                        // 3.0
println(area(h = 2, w = 5))             // 10.0

val double: Int => Int = x => x * 2
val add = (a: Int, b: Int) => a + b
println(List(1, 2, 3).map(double))      // List(2, 4, 6)
println(List(1, 2, 3).map(_ + 10))      // List(11, 12, 13)
println(List(4, 5).reduce(add))         // 9

def twice(f: Int => Int, x: Int): Int = f(f(x))
println(twice(_ * 3, 2))                // 18

def logIf(enabled: Boolean)(msg: => String): Unit =
  if enabled then println(msg)
logIf(false) { println("never evaluated"); "expensive" }
logIf(true)("cheap")                    // cheap

def sum(xs: Int*): Int = xs.sum
println(sum(1, 2, 3) + sum(List(4, 5)*))  // 15
takeaways: `def` defines methods; named and default arguments make calls clear
Lambdas: `x => x * 2` or the placeholder `_ * 2`
`=> A` parameters are by-name, evaluated only when used
Methods turn into functions automatically when needed
pitfalls: Using `_` twice expecting the same argument: `_ * _` is a two-argument function.

quiz.q: What does List(1, 2).map(_ * _) do?
options: Fails to compile: _ * _ takes two arguments
quiz.explain: Each underscore is a separate parameter, so _ * _ is (a, b) => a * b, which doesn't fit map.

concepts.name: Classes, objects and companions
concepts.summary: Define classes with constructor parameters, singleton objects and companion objects.
concepts.why: Classes and objects organise state and behaviour in every Scala codebase.
concepts.body:
A **class** declares its primary constructor in the header: `class Account(val owner: String, private var balance: Double)`. A `val` parameter becomes a public read-only field, `var` a mutable one, and a plain parameter is private to the class. The class body runs as part of the constructor, so `require(balance >= 0)` there validates input. In Scala 3 `new` is optional: `Account("ana", 10)` works.

Members are public by default; `private` and `protected` restrict them, and `private[pkg]` opens access to a package. Auxiliary constructors (`def this(...)`) exist but default parameters usually make them unnecessary.

An **object** is a singleton: one instance, created lazily on first use. Use it for utilities, constants and entry points.

An object with the same name as a class in the same file is its **companion**. They can access each other's private members, and the companion is the conventional home for **factory methods** (`apply`) and constants. `Account.empty("bo")` reads better than a constructor, and a private constructor plus a companion `apply` lets you validate or cache instances.

Methods that take one argument can be written infix (`a max b`), and symbolic names are allowed (`def +(other: Money)`), though libraries use them sparingly. `override def toString` customises printing.
concepts.code:
class Account(val owner: String, private var balance: Double):
  require(balance >= 0, "negative balance")
  def deposit(amount: Double): Unit = balance += amount
  def current: Double = balance
  override def toString = s"Account($owner, $balance)"

object Account:
  private var created = 0
  def empty(owner: String): Account =
    created += 1
    Account(owner, 0)
  def count: Int = created

object MathUtil:
  val Tau = 2 * math.Pi
  def clamp(x: Int, lo: Int, hi: Int) = x max lo min hi

@main def demo(): Unit =
  val a = Account.empty("ana")
  a.deposit(25)
  println(a)                          // Account(ana, 25.0)
  println(a.current)                  // 25.0
  println(Account.count)              // 1
  println(MathUtil.clamp(15, 0, 10))  // 10
  // a.balance                        // error: balance is private
takeaways: Constructor parameters with `val`/`var` become fields
An `object` is a lazily created singleton
A companion object shares privates with its class and holds factories
`new` is optional in Scala 3
pitfalls: Leaving a field as a plain constructor parameter and then trying to read it from outside the class.

quiz.q: class Point(x: Int) declares x without val. Can other code read p.x?
options: Only the companion object can, by default
No, it's private to the class
quiz.explain: A parameter without val or var is not a public member; add val to expose it.

concepts.name: Case classes
concepts.summary: Immutable data classes with structural equality, copy, toString and pattern matching for free.
concepts.why: Case classes are how Scala models data: records, messages, events, DTOs.
concepts.code:
case class Point(x: Int, y: Int):
  def +(o: Point): Point = Point(x + o.x, y + o.y)

case class User(name: String, email: String, active: Boolean = true)

val p = Point(1, 2)
val q = Point(1, 2)
println(p == q)                      // true (structural)
println(p eq q)                      // false (different objects)
println(p + Point(10, 10))           // Point(11,12)

val u = User("ana", "ana@example.com")
val inactive = u.copy(active = false)
println(inactive)                    // User(ana,ana@example.com,false)

val seen = Set(p, q, Point(0, 0))
println(seen.size)                   // 2

p match
  case Point(0, y) => println(s"on the y axis at $y")
  case Point(x, y) => println(s"at $x, $y")   // at 1, 2

println(u.productElementNames.toList)  // List(name, email, active)
takeaways: `case class` = immutable fields + structural equality + copy + pattern matching
Update by `copy(field = value)`
Safe as Map keys and Set elements
Model variants with sealed traits or enums, not case-class inheritance
pitfalls: Putting `var` fields in a case class used as a Map key; mutating it breaks hashing.

quiz.q: case class P(x: Int). What is P(1) == P(1)?
options: true only if both are vals
quiz.explain: Case classes generate equals and hashCode based on their fields.

concepts.name: Pattern matching
concepts.summary: Use match expressions with literal, type, constructor, tuple and guard patterns.
concepts.why: Pattern matching is Scala's main way to branch on the shape of data.
concepts.body:
A **match expression** tests a value against patterns in order and evaluates the first matching case: `x match { case pattern => result ... }`. It's an expression, so it returns a value.

Pattern kinds:

- **Literals**: `case 0 =>`, `case "quit" =>`.
- **Variables** and the wildcard: `case n =>` binds anything to `n`; `case _ =>` matches anything without binding.
- **Types**: `case s: String =>` matches and casts in one step.
- **Constructors** of case classes, nested freely: `case Order(id, Customer(name, _)) =>`.
- **Tuples** and **sequences**: `case (a, b) =>`, `case List(first, rest*) =>`, `case head :: tail =>`.
- **Alternatives** `case 1 | 2 =>` and **binders** `case p @ Point(0, _) =>`.

A **guard** adds a condition: `case n if n < 0 =>`. If no case matches, a `MatchError` is thrown at runtime, which is why matching on a `sealed` hierarchy or enum is preferred: the compiler then warns when a case is missing.

Variable patterns start with a lowercase letter. To compare against an existing value instead of binding a new name, use backticks (`` case `expected` => ``) or an uppercase constant.

Patterns also work in `val` definitions (`val (q, r) = (7 / 2, 7 % 2)`), in `for` generators and in lambdas passed to `collect`.
concepts.code:
case class Customer(name: String, vip: Boolean)
case class Order(id: Int, customer: Customer, total: Double)

def describe(x: Any): String = x match
  case 0                         => "zero"
  case n: Int if n < 0           => s"negative int $n"
  case n: Int                    => s"int $n"
  case s: String                 => s"string of length ${s.length}"
  case (a, b)                    => s"pair $a and $b"
  case List(first, rest*)        => s"list starting $first, ${rest.size} more"
  case Order(id, Customer(name, true), _) => s"VIP order $id for $name"
  case _                         => "something else"

println(describe(-4))                         // negative int -4
println(describe("hey"))                      // string of length 3
println(describe((1, "a")))                   // pair 1 and a
println(describe(List(9, 8, 7)))              // list starting 9, 2 more
println(describe(Order(7, Customer("Ana", true), 99.0)))  // VIP order 7 for Ana
println(describe(3.5))                        // something else

val (q, r) = (17 / 5, 17 % 5)
println(s"$q remainder $r")                   // 3 remainder 2
takeaways: Cases are tried top to bottom; the first match wins
Patterns destructure case classes, tuples and sequences, with guards
Lowercase names bind; use backticks to compare to an existing value
Unmatched values throw MatchError
pitfalls: Writing `case expected =>` meaning the variable `expected`: it creates a new binding that matches everything.

quiz.q: val limit = 10; 5 match { case limit => "hit"; case _ => "miss" } returns?
options: "hit", because limit is a new variable pattern
quiz.explain: A lowercase identifier in a pattern binds a new variable; use `limit` in backticks to compare.

concepts.name: Immutable collections
concepts.summary: List, Vector, Set and Map, and the core transformations map, filter and foldLeft.
concepts.why: Collections and their higher-order methods are what most everyday Scala code is made of.
concepts.body:
Scala's default collections are **immutable**: operations return new collections and the old ones stay valid, safe to share across threads. The main types:

- `List` is a singly linked list: O(1) prepend with `::`, linear indexing. Great for recursion and head/tail processing.
- `Vector` is an indexed sequence with fast (effectively constant) access and update anywhere: the default general-purpose `Seq`.
- `Set` holds unique elements; `Map` holds key-value pairs, built with `"a" -> 1` tuples.
- `Range` (`1 to 10`) and `Array` (mutable, JVM array) complete the picture.

All share a uniform API:

- `map`, `filter`, `flatMap`, `collect` transform;
- `foldLeft(z)(op)`, `sum`, `max`, `count`, `exists`, `forall`, `find` reduce or search;
- `groupBy`, `partition`, `zip`, `sortBy`, `distinct`, `take`, `drop` reshape.

Maps return `Option` from `get`, use `getOrElse` for defaults, and `updated` or `+` to add entries. `map(key)` throws if the key is missing.

Chaining these methods replaces most loops: describe what you want instead of how to iterate. `toList`, `toVector`, `toSet` and `toMap` convert between types.
concepts.code:
val nums = List(5, 3, 8, 1)
println(0 :: nums)                          // List(0, 5, 3, 8, 1)
println(nums.map(_ * 2).filter(_ > 5))      // List(10, 6, 16)
println(nums.foldLeft(0)(_ + _))            // 17
println(nums.sorted.take(2))                // List(1, 3)
println(nums.exists(_ > 7))                 // true

val v = Vector("a", "b", "c")
println(v.updated(1, "B"))                  // Vector(a, B, c)
println(v)                                  // Vector(a, b, c) (unchanged)

val ages = Map("ana" -> 31, "bo" -> 25)
println(ages.get("cy"))                     // None
println(ages.getOrElse("cy", 0))            // 0
println(ages + ("cy" -> 40))                // Map(ana -> 31, bo -> 25, cy -> 40)

val words = List("apple", "avocado", "banana", "cherry")
println(words.groupBy(_.head).view.mapValues(_.size).toMap)
// Map(a -> 2, b -> 1, c -> 1) (order may vary)
println(words.partition(_.length > 5))      // (List(avocado, banana, cherry),List(apple))
takeaways: Default collections are immutable: operations return new ones
List for head/tail and prepend, Vector for indexed access
map, filter, foldLeft, groupBy and friends replace loops
`Map.get` returns an Option; `map(key)` throws if missing
pitfalls: Using `list(i)` in a loop over a List, which is O(n) per access; use a Vector or iterate.

quiz.q: Which collection gives fast random access by index?
quiz.explain: Vector is a tree-based indexed sequence with effectively constant-time access; List access is linear.

concepts.name: Traits and mixins
concepts.summary: Define interfaces with abstract and concrete members, and mix several traits into a class.
concepts.why: Traits are Scala's tool for abstraction, code reuse and modular design.
concepts.body:
A **trait** declares abstract members (methods, values, types) and can also provide concrete implementations. Classes and objects **extend** one class and any number of traits: `class Duck extends Animal, Swimmer, Flyer` (Scala 3 syntax; `with` also works).

Use traits to:

- define interfaces (`trait Repository[A] { def find(id: Long): Option[A] }`),
- share behaviour (a `Logging` trait with a concrete `log` method),
- stack modifications (several traits overriding the same method and calling `super`).

When multiple traits define the same method, Scala uses **linearization**: the class and its traits are put in a single order (roughly right to left) and `super` calls the next one in that order. This gives predictable stackable behaviour, unlike the diamond problem in some languages.

Scala 3 traits can take **parameters** (`trait Greeting(val name: String)`), which only the class that first mixes it in passes.

Use an **abstract class** instead when you need Java interoperability with constructors or when a type is clearly a base implementation. Otherwise prefer traits.

Mark a trait `sealed` when all implementations live in the same file: then the compiler knows every subtype, enabling exhaustive pattern matching (next lesson).
concepts.code:
trait Shape:
  def area: Double                       // abstract
  def describe: String = f"${getClass.getSimpleName} with area $area%.2f"

trait Logged extends Shape:
  override def describe: String = "[log] " + super.describe

trait Loud extends Shape:
  override def describe: String = super.describe.toUpperCase

class Circle(r: Double) extends Shape:
  def area = math.Pi * r * r

class Square(s: Double) extends Shape, Loud, Logged:
  def area = s * s

trait Greeting(val greeting: String):
  def greet(n: String) = s"$greeting, $n"
object Formal extends Greeting("Good day")

@main def traitsDemo(): Unit =
  println(Circle(1).describe)      // Circle with area 3.14
  println(Square(2).describe)      // [log] SQUARE WITH AREA 4.00
  println(Formal.greet("Ana"))     // Good day, Ana
takeaways: Traits mix abstract and concrete members; a class can extend many
Linearization orders traits; `super` calls the next in line
Scala 3 traits can take parameters
`sealed` traits enable exhaustive matching
pitfalls: Assuming trait order doesn't matter: `extends A, B` and `extends B, A` can behave differently.

quiz.q: Square extends Shape, Loud, Logged, both overriding describe and calling super. Which runs first?
quiz.explain: Linearization puts the rightmost trait first, so Logged runs and its super is Loud.

concepts.name: Enums and algebraic data types
concepts.summary: Model closed sets of alternatives with enum and sealed traits, and match on them exhaustively.
concepts.why: ADTs let the compiler prove you've handled every case, eliminating whole classes of bugs.
concepts.body:
An **algebraic data type** (ADT) is a type defined as one of a fixed set of alternatives, each possibly carrying data. Scala 3's `enum` expresses them directly:

- A simple enumeration: `enum Color { case Red, Green, Blue }` with `Color.values`, `Color.valueOf("Red")` and `ordinal`.
- Enums can have parameters and members: `enum Planet(val mass: Double) { case Earth extends Planet(5.97e24) ... }`.
- Cases can carry their own data, making a full ADT: `enum Shape { case Circle(r: Double); case Rect(w: Double, h: Double) }`.
- Enums can be generic: the standard `Option` could be written `enum Option[+A] { case Some(x: A); case None }`.

The equivalent in Scala 2 style, still common and sometimes more flexible, is a `sealed trait` with `case class` and `case object` subtypes in the same file.

Because the set of cases is closed, a `match` that misses one produces a compiler **warning** ("match may not be exhaustive"). Treat it as an error (`-Werror`) and you get a compile-time checklist whenever a new case is added.

Design tip: make illegal states unrepresentable. Instead of a class with nullable fields and a `status` string, define an enum where each case has exactly the data that state needs.
concepts.code:
enum Color:
  case Red, Green, Blue

enum Payment:
  case Card(number: String, expiry: String)
  case Transfer(iban: String)
  case Cash

import Payment.*

def fee(p: Payment, amount: Double): Double = p match
  case Card(_, _)  => amount * 0.02
  case Transfer(_) => 0.5
  case Cash        => 0.0
  // removing a case gives: "match may not be exhaustive"

@main def enums(): Unit =
  println(Color.values.toList)             // List(Red, Green, Blue)
  println(Color.valueOf("Green").ordinal)  // 1
  val payments = List(Card("4242", "12/29"), Transfer("AM00"), Cash)
  println(payments.map(fee(_, 100)))       // List(2.0, 0.5, 0.0)
  println(Transfer("X"))                   // Transfer(X)
takeaways: `enum` models a closed set of cases, with or without data
Sealed traits plus case classes are the equivalent older encoding
Exhaustiveness checking warns when a case is missing
Make illegal states unrepresentable
pitfalls: Adding a wildcard `case _` to every match, which silences exhaustiveness warnings when new cases are added.

quiz.q: Why prefer an enum over a String status field?
options: The compiler checks that matches handle every case
quiz.explain: A closed enum lets the compiler warn about unhandled cases, which a free-form String can't.

concepts.name: Option, Either and Try
concepts.summary: Represent missing values and failures as data with Option, Either and Try instead of null and exceptions.
concepts.why: Typed error handling makes failure paths visible in signatures and composable.
concepts.body:
Idiomatic Scala avoids `null` and avoids exceptions for expected failures. Three types make absence and failure explicit:

- `Option[A]` is `Some(a)` or `None`. Use it for values that may be missing: `map.get(key)`, `list.find(...)`, `headOption`. Wrap Java values that may be null with `Option(x)`.
- `Either[E, A]` is `Left(error)` or `Right(value)`. It is right-biased: `map` and `flatMap` work on the `Right` and pass a `Left` through unchanged. Use it when the caller needs to know **why** something failed, with a typed error (often an enum).
- `Try[A]` is `Success(a)` or `Failure(throwable)`. `Try(expr)` catches non-fatal exceptions, which makes it the bridge from exception-throwing (often Java) code.

All three share an API: `map`, `flatMap`, `filter`, `getOrElse`, `fold`, `foreach` and conversions like `toOption`, `toEither` and `toRight(err)`. Pattern matching works too.

Don't call `.get` on an `Option` or `Try`: it throws when empty and defeats the purpose. Chain transformations and decide at the edge of the program what to do with the error. Chaining several steps that can fail is cleanest with a `for` comprehension (next lesson).
concepts.code:
import scala.util.{Try, Success, Failure}

val ages = Map("ana" -> 31)
println(ages.get("ana").map(_ + 1))         // Some(32)
println(ages.get("bo").getOrElse(0))        // 0
println(Option(null: String))               // None

enum ParseError:
  case Empty
  case NotANumber(input: String)

def parse(s: String): Either[ParseError, Int] =
  if s.isEmpty then Left(ParseError.Empty)
  else s.toIntOption.toRight(ParseError.NotANumber(s))

println(parse("42").map(_ * 2))             // Right(84)
println(parse("x4").map(_ * 2))             // Left(NotANumber(x4))
println(parse("").fold(e => s"error: $e", n => s"ok $n"))  // error: Empty

val t = Try("12a".toInt)
t match
  case Success(n)  => println(n)
  case Failure(ex) => println(ex.getClass.getSimpleName)  // NumberFormatException
println(Try(10 / 2).toOption)               // Some(5)
takeaways: `Option` for absence, `Either` for typed errors, `Try` to catch exceptions
All support map, flatMap, getOrElse and fold
Either is right-biased: map works on the success value
Never call `.get`; handle the empty case explicitly
pitfalls: Wrapping everything in Try, losing the specific error type that Either with an error enum would give.

quiz.q: What does Left("oops").map((x: Int) => x + 1) return?
quiz.explain: Either is right-biased: map transforms only a Right and passes a Left through unchanged.

concepts.name: For comprehensions
concepts.summary: Chain flatMap, map and withFilter readably over Options, Eithers, collections and Futures.
concepts.why: For comprehensions make multi-step logic over effect types read like sequential code.
concepts.body:
A `for` comprehension with `yield` is syntax sugar for calls to `flatMap`, `map` and `withFilter`. The compiler rewrites

```scala
for a <- fa; b <- fb(a) yield f(a, b)
```

into `fa.flatMap(a => fb(a).map(b => f(a, b)))`. Any type with those methods works, which is why the same syntax handles collections, `Option`, `Either`, `Try`, `Future` and effect types like Cats Effect's `IO`.

With `Option` and `Either` it expresses "do these steps in order and stop at the first failure": each `<-` unwraps a value, and if any step yields `None` or `Left`, the whole expression short-circuits to it.

Other parts:

- `if cond` guards filter (requires `withFilter`; `Either` doesn't support guards without an empty value).
- `x = expr` binds an intermediate value without unwrapping.
- With collections, multiple generators produce a cartesian product.

All generators in one comprehension must be of the **same kind**: you can't mix `Option` and `List` steps directly; convert first (`opt.toList`, `opt.toRight(err)`).

Without `yield`, a `for` loop desugars to `foreach` and returns `Unit`.
concepts.code:
case class User(id: Int, name: String, managerId: Option[Int])
val users = Map(1 -> User(1, "Ana", None), 2 -> User(2, "Bo", Some(1)))

def managerName(id: Int): Option[String] =
  for
    user    <- users.get(id)
    mgrId   <- user.managerId
    manager <- users.get(mgrId)
  yield manager.name

println(managerName(2))   // Some(Ana)
println(managerName(1))   // None (Ana has no manager)

def toAge(s: String): Either[String, Int] = s.toIntOption.toRight(s"bad: $s")
val total = for
  a <- toAge("30")
  b <- toAge("x")
  sum = a + b
yield sum
println(total)            // Left(bad: x)

val pairs = for n <- List(1, 2, 3); c <- List('a', 'b') if n != 2 yield s"$n$c"
println(pairs)            // List(1a, 1b, 3a, 3b)
takeaways: `for ... yield` desugars to flatMap/map/withFilter
Over Option/Either it short-circuits at the first None/Left
All generators must be the same kind of type
`x = expr` binds a plain intermediate value
pitfalls: Mixing an Option generator into a List comprehension (or Future with Option) and getting confusing type errors.

quiz.q: What does for { a <- Some(1); b <- None: Option[Int] } yield a + b return?
quiz.explain: The second step is None, so flatMap short-circuits and the result is None.

concepts.name: Higher-order functions and currying
concepts.summary: Write functions that take or return functions, curry parameter lists and compose behaviour.
concepts.why: Higher-order functions remove duplication and are the core of functional design in Scala.
concepts.body:
A **higher-order function** takes a function as a parameter or returns one. `map`, `filter` and `foldLeft` are examples; writing your own lets you abstract over behaviour, not just values: `def retry[A](n: Int)(action: => A): A`, `def timed[A](label: String)(body: => A): A`.

Returning functions builds behaviour from parts: `def multiplier(k: Int): Int => Int = x => x * k`. The returned function is a **closure** that captures `k`.

**Currying** means splitting parameters into separate lists: `def add(a: Int)(b: Int) = a + b`. Supplying the first list gives a function waiting for the rest: `val inc = add(1)` (in Scala 3 this eta-expands automatically). Multiple parameter lists also help type inference: in `foldLeft(0)(_ + _)` the type `Int` is fixed by the first list before the lambda is checked. A function value can be curried with `.curried` and uncurried with `Function.uncurried`.

Composition combines functions: `f andThen g` applies f then g, `f compose g` applies g then f.

**Partial functions** (`PartialFunction[A, B]`) are defined only for some inputs, written as a block of `case` clauses. `collect` uses them to filter and map in one step, and `isDefinedAt` checks the domain.

Prefer small, pure functions combined this way; they're trivially testable.
concepts.code:
def multiplier(k: Int): Int => Int = x => x * k
val triple = multiplier(3)
println(triple(5))                               // 15

def add(a: Int)(b: Int): Int = a + b
val inc = add(1)
println(List(1, 2, 3).map(inc))                  // List(2, 3, 4)

val trim: String => String = _.trim
val shout: String => String = _.toUpperCase + "!"
println((trim andThen shout)("  hi "))           // HI!

def retry[A](times: Int)(action: => A): A =
  try action
  catch case e: Exception if times > 1 => retry(times - 1)(action)

var attempts = 0
val result = retry(3) { attempts += 1; if attempts < 3 then sys.error("fail") else "ok" }
println(s"$result after $attempts attempts")     // ok after 3 attempts

val parseEven: PartialFunction[String, Int] = {
  case s if s.toIntOption.exists(_ % 2 == 0) => s.toInt
}
println(List("2", "x", "7", "10").collect(parseEven))  // List(2, 10)
takeaways: Functions can take and return functions (closures capture values)
Multiple parameter lists enable currying and better type inference
`andThen`/`compose` chain functions
`collect` with a partial function filters and maps at once
pitfalls: Calling a partial function on an input it's not defined for, which throws MatchError; check isDefinedAt or use lift.

quiz.q: val f = (x: Int) => x + 1; val g = (x: Int) => x * 2. What is (f andThen g)(3)?
quiz.explain: andThen applies f first (3 + 1 = 4), then g (4 * 2 = 8).

concepts.name: Collections in depth: views and mutability
concepts.summary: Pick the right collection for performance, use views and LazyList for laziness, and use mutable collections deliberately.
concepts.why: Choosing collections well matters for performance and memory in real workloads.
concepts.body:
The collections library is a hierarchy: `Iterable` at the top, then `Seq` (ordered, with `IndexedSeq` like `Vector`/`ArraySeq` and `LinearSeq` like `List`), `Set` and `Map`. Code against the most general type that fits (`Seq[A]`, `Iterable[A]`), and pick the concrete one for its performance:

- `List`: O(1) prepend/head/tail, O(n) index and append.
- `Vector`: effectively constant index, update, append and prepend.
- `ArraySeq`/`Array`: compact and fastest for primitives; `Array` is mutable.
- `HashMap`/`HashSet` default; `TreeMap`/`TreeSet` keep keys sorted; `ListMap` keeps insertion order but is slow (the default immutable `Map` keeps insertion order only up to 4 entries).

Chained operations like `xs.map(f).filter(p).take(10)` build an intermediate collection at each step. A **view** (`xs.view.map(f).filter(p).take(10).toList`) fuses them lazily and computes only what's needed. `LazyList` is a lazily evaluated, memoised sequence that can be infinite; `Iterator` is a one-shot lazy stream.

**Mutable** collections (`scala.collection.mutable.ArrayBuffer`, `HashMap`, `ListBuffer`) are fine for local, performance-sensitive building; keep them private and expose immutable results (`buf.toList`). The `scala.jdk.CollectionConverters` import adds `.asScala`/`.asJava` for Java interop.
concepts.code:
import scala.collection.mutable

val evens = LazyList.from(1).filter(_ % 2 == 0)
println(evens.take(5).toList)                   // List(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)

var calls = 0
val r = (1 to 1_000_000).view
  .map { x => calls += 1; x * x }
  .filter(_ % 7 == 0)
  .take(3)
  .toList
println(s"$r after $calls calls")               // List(49, 196, 441) after 21 calls

val buf = mutable.ArrayBuffer.empty[Int]
for i <- 1 to 5 do buf += i * 10
val frozen: Vector[Int] = buf.toVector          // expose immutable
println(frozen)                                 // Vector(10, 20, 30, 40, 50)

val counts = mutable.Map.empty[Char, Int].withDefaultValue(0)
"mississippi".foreach(c => counts(c) += 1)
println(counts.toSeq.sortBy(-_._2).head)        // (i,4) or (s,4)

val sorted = collection.immutable.TreeMap(3 -> "c", 1 -> "a", 2 -> "b")
println(sorted.keys.toList)                     // List(1, 2, 3)
takeaways: Code against Seq/Iterable; choose List, Vector or ArraySeq for performance
Views and LazyList avoid intermediate collections
Mutable collections for local building, immutable results outward
TreeMap for sorted keys; default Map order is not guaranteed
pitfalls: Relying on the iteration order of a default immutable Map or Set with more than four elements.

quiz.q: Why use .view before a chain of map/filter/take?
options: To avoid building intermediate collections and compute only what's needed
quiz.explain: A view fuses the operations lazily, so only the elements required by take are processed.

concepts.name: sbt projects and testing with MUnit
concepts.summary: Structure a project with build.sbt, add dependencies with %%, and write tests with MUnit.
concepts.why: Real projects need a build, dependencies and tests; sbt is the most widely used Scala build tool.
concepts.body:
**sbt** is the standard Scala build tool. A minimal project is a `build.sbt` plus `project/build.properties` (pinning the sbt version) and sources under `src/main/scala` and tests under `src/test/scala`. Start the sbt shell once with `sbt` and run tasks inside it, keeping the JVM warm: `compile`, `run`, `test`, `testOnly *ParserSuite`, `console` and `~test` (rerun on file changes).

Dependencies use the form `"org" %% "artifact" % "version"`. The double `%%` appends the Scala binary version (`_3`) to the artifact name, picking the build for your Scala version; a single `%` is for plain Java libraries. Test-only libraries get `% Test`. Multi-module builds define several projects with `lazy val core = project.in(file("core"))` and `dependsOn`.

**MUnit** is a lightweight testing library that works with sbt and Scala CLI. A test suite extends `munit.FunSuite` and declares `test("name") { ... }` blocks with `assertEquals(obtained, expected)`, `assert(cond)` and `intercept[Ex] { ... }`. It prints readable diffs on failure. ScalaTest is the older, larger alternative, and ScalaCheck adds property-based tests.

For single-file work, Scala CLI handles tests too: files ending in `.test.scala` with `//> using test.dep org.scalameta::munit::1.1.0` run with `scala test .`.
takeaways: build.sbt declares settings; run tasks in the sbt shell
`%%` picks the artifact built for your Scala version; `% Test` scopes it
MUnit: extend FunSuite, write `test(...)` with assertEquals
`~test` reruns tests on every save
pitfalls: Using a single % for a Scala library, which fails to resolve or pulls in the wrong binary version.

quiz.q: What does %% do in "org.scalameta" %% "munit" % "1.1.0"?
options: Appends the Scala binary version suffix to the artifact name
quiz.explain: %% resolves munit_3 for Scala 3 projects, matching the library build to your Scala version.

concepts.name: Generics, variance and bounds
concepts.summary: Type parameters, covariance (+A), contravariance (-A) and upper/lower bounds.
concepts.why: Variance determines when a container of a subtype can be used as a container of a supertype.
concepts.body:
Classes, traits and methods take **type parameters**: `class Box[A](value: A)`, `def first[A](xs: List[A]): Option[A]`. The compiler infers them at call sites.

**Variance** describes how subtyping of the parameter relates to subtyping of the generic type, given `Cat <: Animal`:

- **Covariant** `+A`: `List[Cat] <: List[Animal]`. Right for immutable producers: `List`, `Option`, `Vector`, `Either`.
- **Contravariant** `-A`: `Printer[Animal] <: Printer[Cat]`. Right for consumers: a function that accepts any `Animal` can be used where one accepting `Cat` is needed. `Function1[-A, +B]` is contravariant in input and covariant in output.
- **Invariant** (no annotation): no relationship. Required for mutable containers: `Array[Cat]` must not be an `Array[Animal]`, or you could put a `Dog` into it.

The compiler checks variance positions: a covariant type can't appear as a method parameter. The fix is a **lower bound**: `def prepend[B >: A](b: B): List[B]` widens the element type as needed, which is how `List` lets you add an `Animal` to a `List[Cat]`.

**Upper bounds** `A <: Comparable[A]` restrict a parameter to subtypes. Prefer type classes (`using Ordering[A]`) for capabilities like ordering, because they work for types you don't control.

Type parameters are **erased** at runtime on the JVM: `List[Int]` and `List[String]` are the same class, so `case xs: List[Int]` can't be checked. A `ClassTag` or `TypeTest` recovers some information when needed.
concepts.code:
sealed trait Animal { def name: String }
case class Cat(name: String) extends Animal
case class Dog(name: String) extends Animal

final case class Box[+A](value: A):
  def map[B](f: A => B): Box[B] = Box(f(value))
  def orElse[B >: A](other: B): List[B] = List(value, other)  // lower bound

trait Printer[-A]:
  def print(a: A): String

val animalPrinter: Printer[Animal] = a => s"animal ${a.name}"
val catPrinter: Printer[Cat] = animalPrinter      // OK: contravariance

val catBox: Box[Cat] = Box(Cat("Tom"))
val animalBox: Box[Animal] = catBox               // OK: covariance
println(animalBox.map(_.name))                    // Box(Tom)
println(catBox.orElse(Dog("Rex")))                // List(Cat(Tom), Dog(Rex))
println(catPrinter.print(Cat("Kit")))             // animal Kit

def maxOf[A <: Comparable[A]](a: A, b: A): A = if a.compareTo(b) >= 0 then a else b
println(maxOf("pear", "apple"))                   // pear
// val arr: Array[Animal] = Array[Cat]()          // error: Array is invariant
takeaways: `+A` covariant for producers, `-A` contravariant for consumers, invariant for mutable
Use a lower bound `B >: A` to accept wider types in covariant classes
Upper bounds `A <: T` restrict; type classes are often better
Generics are erased at runtime
pitfalls: Matching `case xs: List[Int]` and expecting the element type to be checked; it's erased.

quiz.q: Why is Array invariant while List is covariant?
options: Arrays are mutable, so covariance would allow writing a Dog into an Array[Cat]
It's a historical accident with no reason
quiz.explain: Mutable containers both read and write elements, so only invariance is type-safe.

concepts.name: Givens, using clauses and type classes
concepts.summary: Contextual abstractions: provide instances with given, require them with using, and build type classes.
concepts.why: Type classes power JSON codecs, ordering, numeric abstraction and every major functional library.
concepts.body:
Scala 3 **contextual abstractions** let the compiler pass arguments for you based on their type.

- A `given` defines a canonical instance of a type: `given Ordering[Version] = Ordering.by(v => (v.major, v.minor))`.
- A `using` clause declares a parameter the compiler fills in from givens in scope: `def sortAll[A](xs: List[A])(using ord: Ordering[A])`. Callers write `sortAll(versions)`, or pass one explicitly with `sortAll(versions)(using reverseOrd)`.
- A **context bound** is shorthand: `def sortAll[A: Ordering](xs: List[A])`, and `summon[Ordering[A]]` retrieves the instance.

Together these implement **type classes**: a trait describing a capability (`trait Show[A] { def show(a: A): String }`), given instances for each type, and generic functions requiring the capability. Unlike inheritance, you can add a capability to types you don't own (`Int`, `java.time.Instant`) and choose different instances in different scopes.

Where does the compiler look? In the lexical scope (including imports) and in the **implicit scope** of the involved types: companion objects of `Show`, of `A`, and of their parts. Put instances for your own types in their companions and they're found without imports. Importing givens needs the special form `import mylib.given`.

`derives Show` on a case class auto-generates an instance when the type class supports derivation.
concepts.code:
trait Show[A]:
  def show(a: A): String

object Show:
  given Show[Int] with
    def show(n: Int) = s"#$n"
  given [A](using s: Show[A]): Show[List[A]] with
    def show(xs: List[A]) = xs.map(s.show).mkString("[", ", ", "]")

case class Version(major: Int, minor: Int)
object Version:
  given Ordering[Version] = Ordering.by(v => (v.major, v.minor))
  given Show[Version] = v => s"v${v.major}.${v.minor}"

def describe[A: Show](a: A): String = "value " + summon[Show[A]].show(a)

@main def tc(): Unit =
  println(describe(42))                        // value #42
  println(describe(List(1, 2)))                // value [#1, #2]
  val vs = List(Version(1, 10), Version(1, 2), Version(0, 9))
  println(vs.sorted.map(describe(_)))          // List(value v0.9, value v1.2, value v1.10)
  println(vs.max)                              // Version(1,10)
  val newestFirst = summon[Ordering[Version]].reverse
  println(vs.sorted(using newestFirst).head)   // Version(1,10)
takeaways: `given` provides an instance; `using` requires one
Context bounds `[A: Show]` plus `summon` are shorthand
Type classes add capabilities to types you don't own
Companion objects are searched automatically; others need `import x.given`
pitfalls: Defining givens in an unrelated object and forgetting `import thatObject.given`; a normal wildcard import doesn't bring givens.

quiz.q: Where should a given Ordering[Version] live so that it's found without imports?
options: In the companion object of Version
quiz.explain: The implicit scope of a type includes its companion object, so instances there are always found.

concepts.name: Extension methods
concepts.summary: Add methods to existing types with extension, and combine them with type classes for fluent syntax.
concepts.why: Extensions give readable APIs on types you don't control without wrappers or inheritance.
concepts.body:
An **extension method** adds a method to a type after the fact:

```scala
extension (s: String) def words: List[String] = s.split("\\s+").toList
```

Now `"a b c".words` works anywhere the extension is in scope. Several methods can share one clause with an indented block, type parameters are allowed (`extension [A](xs: List[A]) def second: Option[A]`), and operators can be defined too.

The compiler finds an extension when it's visible by name (defined or imported in scope) or when it's defined in a given instance or companion object in the implicit scope of the receiver's type. This makes extensions a natural partner for **type classes**: define them inside the type class trait and every type with an instance gets the syntax:

```scala
trait Show[A]:
  extension (a: A) def show: String
```

Under the hood an extension is just a method with the receiver as an extra first parameter; there's no wrapper allocation, so it's free at runtime.

Extensions can't override existing methods: if the type already has a member with that name, the real member wins. Use them for convenience and domain-specific syntax, and keep them discoverable by putting them next to the types or type classes they extend.
concepts.code:
extension (s: String)
  def words: List[String] = s.trim.split("\\s+").toList
  def isPalindrome: Boolean =
    val c = s.toLowerCase.filter(_.isLetter)
    c == c.reverse

extension [A](xs: List[A])
  def second: Option[A] = xs.drop(1).headOption

case class Money(cents: Long)
extension (m: Money)
  def +(o: Money): Money = Money(m.cents + o.cents)
  def pretty: String = f"$$${m.cents / 100.0}%.2f"

trait Show[A]:
  extension (a: A) def show: String
given Show[Boolean] with
  extension (b: Boolean) def show = if b then "yes" else "no"

@main def ext(): Unit =
  println("  to be  or not ".words)           // List(to, be, or, not)
  println("Never odd or even".isPalindrome)   // true
  println(List(1, 2, 3).second)               // Some(2)
  println((Money(150) + Money(275)).pretty)   // $4.25
  println(true.show)                          // yes
takeaways: `extension (x: T) def m = ...` adds methods to existing types
Extensions inside type classes give syntax to every instance
No runtime wrapper: the receiver is just the first parameter
Existing members always take precedence
pitfalls: Defining an extension with the same name as an existing method and wondering why it's never called.

quiz.q: String already has a method trim. You define extension (s: String) def trim = "x". What does " a ".trim return?
quiz.explain: Real members take precedence over extensions, so String.trim runs.

concepts.name: Futures and asynchronous code
concepts.summary: Run work asynchronously with Future and ExecutionContext, compose results and handle failures.
concepts.why: Services do I/O concurrently; Future is the standard library's basic tool for it.
concepts.body:
A `Future[A]` represents a value that will be available later, computed on a thread pool. `Future { work }` starts the computation immediately on an **ExecutionContext**, which you supply as a `using` parameter; `scala.concurrent.ExecutionContext.Implicits.global` is a reasonable default for CPU-bound work.

Futures compose without blocking:

- `map`, `flatMap` and `for` comprehensions chain dependent steps.
- `Future.sequence(list)` and `Future.traverse` turn many futures into one; `zip` combines two.
- `recover` and `recoverWith` handle failures; a failed future carries the exception, and later steps are skipped.
- `onComplete` registers a callback with a `Try`.

Futures are **eager**: two futures created before a `for` run in parallel, while futures created inside it run sequentially. Start independent work first, then combine.

Never block inside a future-based service. `Await.result(f, 5.seconds)` exists for tests and the top of `main`; elsewhere return the `Future`. Wrap blocking I/O in `blocking { ... }` so the global pool can compensate.

Futures can't be cancelled and they are not referentially transparent (creating one starts work). Larger codebases often use effect systems such as **Cats Effect** or **ZIO**, whose lazy `IO` values add cancellation, resource safety and structured concurrency. Java 21 virtual threads are a simpler alternative for blocking-style code.
concepts.code:
import scala.concurrent.{Future, Await, blocking}
import scala.concurrent.duration.*
import scala.concurrent.ExecutionContext.Implicits.global

def fetchPrice(item: String): Future[Double] = Future {
  blocking(Thread.sleep(200))                    // simulate blocking I/O
  if item == "unknown" then throw IllegalArgumentException(item)
  item.length * 1.5
}

val start = System.nanoTime
val fa = fetchPrice("apple")                     // both start now
val fb = fetchPrice("kiwi")
val total = for a <- fa; b <- fb yield a + b
println(Await.result(total, 2.seconds))          // 13.5
println((System.nanoTime - start) / 1_000_000 < 380)  // true: ran in parallel

val all = Future.traverse(List("fig", "plum"))(fetchPrice)
println(Await.result(all, 2.seconds))            // List(4.5, 6.0)

val safe = fetchPrice("unknown").recover { case _: IllegalArgumentException => 0.0 }
println(Await.result(safe, 2.seconds))           // 0.0
takeaways: `Future { ... }` starts immediately on an ExecutionContext
Compose with map/flatMap/for, traverse and recover
Create independent futures before the for comprehension to run them in parallel
Await only in tests and at the program edge
pitfalls: Creating futures inside a for comprehension and expecting them to run concurrently; each starts after the previous completes.

quiz.q: val r = for a <- Future(slowA()); b <- Future(slowB()) yield a + b. How do slowA and slowB run?
options: Sequentially: slowB's future is created only after slowA completes
Not at all until Await is called
quiz.explain: The second Future is created inside flatMap's callback, so it starts only when the first finishes.

concepts.name: Java interoperability
concepts.summary: Use Java libraries from Scala, convert collections, handle nulls and expose Scala code to Java.
concepts.why: The whole JVM ecosystem is available to Scala, but the seams need care.
concepts.body:
Scala compiles to JVM bytecode, so any Java library is usable directly: `import java.time.LocalDate` and call methods as usual. Java classes are instantiated without `new` in Scala 3 too, Java static methods are called on the class name, and Java getters work with or without parentheses.

The seams to watch:

- **Collections**: Java and Scala collections are different types. `import scala.jdk.CollectionConverters.*` adds `.asScala` and `.asJava`, which wrap without copying.
- **Null**: Java methods may return `null`. Wrap results with `Option(javaCall())`. (The `-Yexplicit-nulls` compiler flag makes the type system track nullable Java types.)
- **Functional interfaces**: Scala lambdas convert automatically to Java SAM types like `Runnable`, `Comparator` or `java.util.function.Function`. `scala.jdk.FunctionConverters` and `scala.jdk.FutureConverters` cover other conversions, and `scala.jdk.OptionConverters` handles `java.util.Optional`.
- **Checked exceptions** don't exist in Scala; use `@throws[IOException]` to declare them for Java callers.
- **Varargs**: annotate with `@varargs` to make a Scala varargs method callable from Java naturally.

Calling Scala from Java is possible but less pleasant: `object` members are reachable through static forwarders, default parameters aren't visible, and Scala collections look odd. For libraries consumed from Java, expose a thin Java-friendly facade.
concepts.code:
import java.time.{LocalDate, DayOfWeek}
import java.util.ArrayList
import scala.jdk.CollectionConverters.*
import scala.jdk.OptionConverters.*

val d = LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 17)
println(d.getDayOfWeek)                          // SATURDAY
println(d.plusDays(2).getDayOfWeek == DayOfWeek.MONDAY)  // true

val jl = ArrayList[String]()
jl.add("pear"); jl.add("fig")
val sl: List[String] = jl.asScala.toList
println(sl.map(_.toUpperCase))                   // List(PEAR, FIG)

jl.sort((a: String, b: String) => a.length - b.length)  // lambda -> Comparator
println(jl)                                      // [fig, pear]

val props = System.getProperties
println(Option(props.getProperty("no.such.key")).getOrElse("default"))  // default
println(java.util.Optional.of(5).toScala)        // Some(5)
println(sl.asJava.isInstanceOf[java.util.List[?]])  // true (a wrapper, no copy)
takeaways: Java classes are used directly; static methods via the class name
`scala.jdk.CollectionConverters` adds `.asScala`/`.asJava` wrappers
Wrap possibly-null Java results in `Option(...)`
Lambdas convert to Java functional interfaces automatically
pitfalls: Passing a Scala List to a Java API expecting java.util.List without `.asJava`.

quiz.q: How do you safely handle a Java method that may return null?
quiz.explain: Option(x) becomes None for null and Some(x) otherwise; Some(null) would keep the null.

concepts.name: Opaque, union and intersection types
concepts.summary: Zero-cost type wrappers with opaque types, and precise types with A | B and A & B.
concepts.why: These Scala 3 features model domains precisely with no runtime overhead.
concepts.body:
An **opaque type alias** creates a new type that is the underlying type at runtime but a distinct type at compile time. Inside its defining scope the alias is transparent; outside, only the API you export is visible:

```scala
object ids:
  opaque type UserId = Long
  object UserId { def apply(n: Long): UserId = n }
```

`UserId` and `Long` can't be mixed up, yet no wrapper object is allocated, unlike a case class wrapper (and unlike Scala 2 value classes, which box in generic contexts). Add operations with extension methods in the same scope, and use the companion to validate (`def from(n: Long): Option[UserId]`).

**Union types** `A | B` say "a value of type A or B". They're unboxed and need no common supertype: `def parse(s: String): Int | ParseError`. Pattern matching narrows them. Unions are also how Scala types literal alternatives: `type Dir = "N" | "S" | "E" | "W"`.

**Intersection types** `A & B` are values that are both: `def save(x: Serializable & Validated)`. They replace Scala 2's compound `with` types and are commutative (`A & B` equals `B & A`).

When inferring the type of a `val` or `def`, the compiler widens a union to a common non-union supertype: `val x = if c then 1 else "a"` doesn't get `Int | String` unless you annotate it, so write the union type where you want one. Opaque types can't be distinguished at runtime, so matching `case id: UserId` is an unchecked type test.
concepts.code:
object units:
  opaque type Meters = Double
  opaque type Seconds = Double
  def meters(d: Double): Meters = d
  def seconds(d: Double): Seconds = d
  extension (m: Meters) def /(s: Seconds): Double = m / s  // inside: Doubles
import units.*
val speed = meters(100) / seconds(9.58)
println(f"$speed%.2f m/s")                  // 10.44 m/s
// meters(1) / 2.0                          // error: found Double, required Seconds
enum ParseError { case Empty, Bad }
def parse(s: String): Int | ParseError =
  if s.isEmpty then ParseError.Empty else s.toIntOption.getOrElse(ParseError.Bad)

for s <- List("42", "", "x") do
  parse(s) match
    case n: Int        => println(s"int $n")
    case e: ParseError => println(s"error $e")   // int 42 / error Empty / error Bad
type Dir = "N" | "S"
val d: Dir = "N"                            // "W" would not compile
trait Named { def name: String }
trait Aged { def age: Int }
def card(p: Named & Aged) = s"${p.name} (${p.age})"
println(card(new Named with Aged { val name = "Ana"; val age = 31 }))  // Ana (31)
takeaways: Opaque types: distinct at compile time, the raw type at runtime
Add operations to opaque types with extensions in their scope
`A | B` unions need no common supertype; match to narrow
`A & B` values satisfy both types
pitfalls: Expecting the compiler to infer `Int | String` for an if/else: annotate the expected union type.

quiz.q: What is the runtime representation of opaque type UserId = Long?
quiz.explain: Opaque types erase to their underlying type, so there's no allocation overhead.

concepts.name: Inline and macros
concepts.summary: Compile-time programming with inline, compiletime ops, quotes and splices.
concepts.why: Libraries use these for zero-overhead abstractions, derivation and compile-time checks.
concepts.body:
Scala 3 has a principled metaprogramming system built in layers.

**`inline`** is the first layer. An `inline def` is guaranteed to be inlined at each call site. Combined with `inline` parameters, `inline if` and `inline match`, the branches are resolved during compilation, so code specialised to constants costs nothing at runtime. `transparent inline` methods may even return a more specific type than declared.

`scala.compiletime` adds tools usable inside inline code: `error("msg")` emits a custom compile error, `constValue[T]` turns a literal type into a value, `erasedValue[T]` lets you match on types, and `summonInline`/`summonFrom` look up givens at expansion time. This is enough for a lot of type-class **derivation** with `scala.deriving.Mirror`.

**Macros** are the second layer. An inline method calls `${ impl('x) }`, and `impl` is a regular method running in the compiler that receives typed code as `Expr[T]` and returns new code built with **quotes** `'{ ... }` and **splices** `${ ... }`. Macros are type-checked, hygienic and, unlike Scala 2 macros, part of the stable language. The **reflection API** (`quotes.reflect`) gives full access to trees when quotes aren't enough.

Rules: a macro implementation must be defined in a different file (compiled earlier) than its call sites, and macros can't introduce new definitions visible to the user's code. Use inline first and reach for macros only when you need to inspect or generate code.
takeaways: `inline` guarantees inlining; `inline if/match` resolve at compile time
`scala.compiletime` gives error, constValue and erasedValue
Macros use quotes `'{}` and splices `${}` over typed `Expr` trees
Macro implementations must be compiled before their call sites
pitfalls: Reaching for macros when an inline method with compiletime operations would do.

quiz.q: What happens when checkedPort(70000) is compiled with the definition above?
options: Compilation fails with "port out of range"
quiz.explain: The inline if is evaluated during compilation and the error branch emits a compile error.

concepts.name: Type-level programming
concepts.summary: Match types, type lambdas, singleton types and tuple operations computed by the compiler.
concepts.why: Type-level computation lets libraries like typed SQL, JSON and data-frame APIs catch errors at compile time.
concepts.body:
Scala 3 can compute **types from types**.

**Match types** are `match` expressions at the type level:

```scala
type Elem[X] = X match
  case String      => Char
  case Array[t]    => t
  case Iterable[t] => t
```

`Elem[List[Int]]` reduces to `Int`. A method returning `Elem[X]` must be implemented with a matching term-level `match` so the compiler can relate the two.

**Type lambdas** `[X] =>> Either[String, X]` are anonymous type constructors, used when a type class expects a one-hole type like `F[_]`. **Higher-kinded types** (`trait Functor[F[_]]`) abstract over containers themselves; this is how Cats and ZIO define `Functor` and `Monad`.

**Singleton and literal types** treat values as types: `3`, `"id"`, `true`. With `scala.compiletime.ops` you can do arithmetic on them (`type Five = 2 + 3`), and `constValue` brings them back as values.

**Tuples** are generic heterogeneous lists in Scala 3 (`*:` and `EmptyTuple`), with type-level operations like `Tuple.Concat`, `Tuple.Map` and `Tuple.Size`; case classes convert to and from tuples via `Mirror`. This is the backbone of generic derivation.

Use these sparingly in application code: compile errors become hard to read and compile times grow. They shine in libraries where precise types prevent misuse.
concepts.code:
import scala.compiletime.ops.int.*
import scala.compiletime.constValue
type Elem[X] = X match
  case String      => Char
  case Array[t]    => t
  case Iterable[t] => t
def first[X](x: X): Elem[X] = x match
  case s: String      => s.charAt(0)
  case a: Array[t]    => a(0)
  case i: Iterable[t] => i.head
trait Functor[F[_]]:
  extension [A](fa: F[A]) def fmap[B](f: A => B): F[B]
given Functor[[X] =>> Either[String, X]] with
  extension [A](fa: Either[String, A]) def fmap[B](f: A => B) = fa.map(f)
@main def typeLevel(): Unit =
  val c: Char = first("scala")
  val n: Int = first(List(7, 8))
  println((c, n))                                  // (s,7)
  println(constValue[3 * 4])                       // 12
  val t = (1, "a", true)
  val t2: (Int, String, Boolean, Double) = t ++ Tuple1(2.5)
  println(t2)                                      // (1,a,true,2.5)
  val r: Either[String, Int] = Right(20)
  println(r.fmap(_ + 1))                           // Right(21)
takeaways: Match types compute result types by matching on type arguments
Type lambdas `[X] =>> F[X]` fill one-hole type parameters
Literal types plus compiletime.ops do arithmetic at compile time
Tuples are type-level lists that power derivation
pitfalls: Writing a method with a match-type result but a body that doesn't mirror the type-level match, causing type errors.

quiz.q: Given type Elem[X] = X match { case String => Char; case Iterable[t] => t }, what is Elem[Vector[Double]]?
quiz.explain: Vector[Double] matches Iterable[t] with t = Double.

concepts.name: Compilation to the JVM and TASTy
concepts.summary: How Scala constructs map to bytecode, what TASTy files are, and the performance consequences.
concepts.why: Knowing what the compiler emits explains boxing, binary compatibility issues and profiler output.
concepts.body:
`scalac` compiles in two outputs: JVM **class files** and **TASTy** files (`.tasty`), a typed abstract syntax tree of every definition. TASTy lets later compilations see full Scala types (including those erased in bytecode), lets Scala 2.13 consume Scala 3 libraries through its TASTy reader, and powers macros and tools like documentation and IDE support.

How constructs map to bytecode:

- A class is a JVM class; a `val` field is a private field plus an accessor method.
- An `object` becomes a class `Name$` with a static `MODULE$` instance, plus static forwarders on `Name` for Java callers.
- A trait becomes a JVM interface with default methods; fields in traits are implemented in the classes that mix them in.
- Lambdas compile via `invokedynamic` and `LambdaMetafactory`, like Java's.
- Top-level definitions go into a synthetic `File$package` object.
- `lazy val` uses a thread-safe initialisation scheme with extra checks on each access.

**Erasure** removes type arguments, so generic code works on `Object`: an `Int` in a `List[Int]` or passed to a generic method is **boxed** to `java.lang.Integer`. Hot numeric code should use `Array[Int]` (a real `int[]`) or specialised structures; opaque types and inline methods avoid boxing that wrappers would add.

**Binary compatibility** is subtle: adding a parameter with a default or a method to a trait can break already compiled code. Library authors check it with MiMa (sbt-mima-plugin). Inspect output with `javap -c -p` on the class files.
concepts.code:
// Wallet.scala, compile with: scala compile Wallet.scala
// then: javap -p -cp <output dir> Wallet Wallet$ Shape
trait Shape:
  def area: Double
  def describe: String = s"area $area"  // -> interface default method

class Wallet(val owner: String):         // -> private field + owner() accessor
  lazy val id: Int = owner.hashCode      // -> guarded lazy initialisation

object Wallet:                           // -> class Wallet$ with MODULE$
  def empty = Wallet("nobody")           //    + static forwarder Wallet.empty()

def sumAll(xs: List[Int]): Int = xs.sum  // top level -> Wallet$package
def sumArray(xs: Array[Int]): Int =      // Array[Int] is a real int[]: no boxing
  var t = 0; var i = 0
  while i < xs.length do { t += xs(i); i += 1 }
  t

@main def jvm(): Unit =
  println(Wallet.empty.owner)            // nobody
  println(sumArray(Array(1, 2, 3)))      // 6
  println(classOf[Wallet].getDeclaredFields.map(_.getName).toList.contains("owner"))  // true
takeaways: Objects compile to `Name$` with a `MODULE$` singleton; traits to interfaces
TASTy files keep full types for later compilation, macros and tools
Erasure boxes primitives in generic code; use arrays for hot numeric loops
Check library binary compatibility with MiMa
pitfalls: Assuming a source-compatible change to a library is also binary compatible.

quiz.q: Why can a List[Int] be slower than an Array[Int] for numeric work?
options: Generic List stores boxed Integer objects due to erasure; Array[Int] is a primitive int[]
quiz.explain: Erasure forces generic collections to hold objects, so each Int is boxed; Array[Int] compiles to int[].
